sum.text: Following last month’s BRICS New Delhi Declaration, India submitted a paper to WTO signaling a willingness to engage in discussions on plurilateral—'coalition of the willing’—agreements. Until now, New Delhi maintained a rigid stance, refusing to negotiate, or even discuss plurilaterals on the grounds that it lacked an explicit mandate to initiate them. Instead, India relied heavily on the letter and spirit of consensus-based decision-making at WTO to assert its legal position. Reactions to India’s submission have been mixed. International partners have been largely sceptical. Optimists view it as a vital opening for constructive dialogue. Pessimists contend that the submission merely repackages New Delhi’s long-standing opposition, serving as a tactical ploy to scuttle progress by insisting on consensus before any discussion can begin. Currently, India is not a participant in any ongoing plurilateral negotiations within WTO. More critically, it has blocked the formal adoption of key outcomes—like the Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD) agreement, and Joint Statement Initiative on e-commerce—into the WTO’s legal framework. India is under no obligation to join these agreements as a member. So it doesn’t take on new obligations. 135001962 But it faces mounting international pressure—including from developing and least developed countries—to lift its veto against their formalisation, an act that requires consensus across the entire membership. To move from obstruction to leadership, India must adopt a constructive stance that protects the multilateral core of the trading system, while enabling modern rulemaking. Plurilateral pathways to multilateralisation are not inherently foreign to WTO. During the GATT Tokyo Round, 7 plurilateral agreements were negotiated, 5 of which were successfully multilateralised during the Uruguay Round that birthed the WTO in 1995. More recently, plurilateral frameworks like Information Technology Agreements (ITA I & II), Financial Services Understanding, and rules on GATS Domestic Regulation were integrated into WTO using specific legal safeguards. points: Capital markets are beginning to price the distance between what artificial intelligence promises and what it earns.

The AI boom now faces eight major risks, divided equally into four financial risks and four beyond the balance sheet.
AI companies are spending heavily on data centres and models in anticipation of future revenues, heavily outrunning actual earnings.
Macroeconomic pressures like the Iran war, high fuel prices, and high US treasury yields are slowing data centre growth.

sum.text:
Capital markets have begun to price the distance between what artificial intelligence (AI) promises and what it earns. Nvidia backed Firmus withdrew a nearly $5 billion initial public offering (IPO) after investors resisted its valuation, and OpenAI and Anthropic postponed their planned trillion dollar listings. The boom now faces eight risks , four financial and four beyond the balance sheet.
What it is: AI companies are spending heavily on models and data centres in expectation of future revenue, like a builder raising towers before buyers have paid.
Hyperscalers: The biggest builders are hyperscalers , cloud companies that run giant data centres AI cannot do without.
Growth outpacing support: AI models are growing faster than the financing , governance and social acceptance they need.
Revenue reset: OpenAI indicated that its September annualised revenue (a month’s earnings scaled to a year) was nearer $50 billion , not the nearly $70 billion signalled earlier.
The takeaway: When revenue lags the money already spent, investors cut valuations, and the debt behind the buildout becomes a risk to lenders.
Macroeconomy: The Iran war , high US gas and diesel prices and the wide US fiscal deficit have pushed treasury yields , the interest the US government pays to borrow, to multi decadal highs. Higher interest rates hurt homebuyers and slow data centre growth.
Revenue trailing capex: Capital expenditure (capex) , spending on long lived assets, is outrunning revenue. Anthropic ran an operating loss of about $8 billion in 2025, so it has little room to raise investors’ expectations.
Costlier, opaque debt: Capex once paid in cash now relies on private credit , loans from funds rather than banks, and bespoke deals, most of them opaque. Most hyperscaler bonds issued in 2026 traded below issue price by end August.
Sobering valuations: OpenAI and Anthropic were reportedly seeking about $60 billion each from their listings. Cautious valuation assessments forced both chief executives to delay.

Opening the high-level meeting at UN Headquarters, General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman evoked the imagery of a wall of water barreling down a mountain valley, sweeping away people, homes and communities in its path.
“ Scientists had long warned that such events were becoming a reality, yet none of us were prepared for the shocking footage ”.
He reminded delegates that this year's strengthening El Niño could be among the strongest since at least 1950, while the world is on its way to hotting up by 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels under current climate policies, far beyond the Paris Agreement 's goals.
“ Behind these figures are families uprooted, children's missing, school women walking farther for water, and communities confronting losses they cannot bear, ” the assembly president added.
The task ahead for world leaders at the upcoming climate conference COP31 is to then turn commitments into action – and promises into trust, he said.
“ COP31 must be more than another negotiating milestone . It must demonstrate that multilateralism delivers.”

The reconstitution was carried out through an official government notification establishing the chairperson and part-time members for a three-year tenure.
FSIB acts as the central headhunter for recommending top-level executive appointments in public sector banks, financial institutions, and insurance firms.
The reconstituted bureau comprises the chairperson and six part-time members drawn from banking, financial regulation, and insurance sectors.
Three members focus on public sector banks and financial institutions: Arijit Basu, Satish Kashinath Marathe, and Ramanathan Subramanian.
Three other members handle state insurance companies: Siddhartha Mohanty, Neerja Kapur, and T L Alamelu.
FSIB also advises the government on transfers, term extensions, service terminations, performance appraisal systems, and codes of conduct.
All recommendations made by FSIB are subject to final approval by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet headed by the Prime Minister.
